newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysian interest rates seen easing in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian interest rates seen easing in 1997.

text.p: A small cut in Malaysian interest rates is possible from the middle of next year if a tighter fiscal policy eases the burden on monetary policy, a Reuters poll of economists said on Thursday.

Economists from 10 research houses in Malaysia and Singapore forecast, on average, that the benchmark three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) would be at 7.21 percent at the end of December this year, down from 7.33 percent on Thursday.
They forecast the three-month KLIBOR at an average 7.18 percent in March, 1997, and at 7.03 percent at the end of the second quarter of next year.

However, the forecasts varied widely. Some economists expected an easing of the country's tight monetary policy next year due to a slowing in economic growth and a shrinkage in the current account gap this year.

"If growth slows down remarkably next year, then we may see the central bank lowering rates, conservatively, from the second quarter (of 1997) onwards," said Chung Tin Fah, general manager of O.S.K. Holdings Bhd.
But he added, "On the cautious side they may maintain rates at the current level."

"If you look at the significant improvement managed on the trade front, and since interest rates tend to follow the current account deficit, there is scope for lowering rates next year," said Tan Min Lan, an economist at Merrill Lynch in Singapore.
Malaysia has recorded a sharply lower trade deficit of 163.2 million ringgit in the first nine months of 1996 against 8.2 billion in the corresponding period of last year.
However, other economists were less optimistic about the prospect of lower rates, citing continued high growth in loans and money supply as factors which could keep rates from falling.

"We don't see much downside (in Malaysian interest rates) given the fact that money supply and credit growth continue to be very high. So far there is no evidence of rates coming down," Chang Kok Peng, economist with Credit Lyonnais in Singapore said.

"With a relatively high savings-investment gap and given the current demand in the economy, it will be good to have a strong ringgit, which implies high interest rates," said Christopher Chong, economist with James Capel in Singapore.

But the majority of economists surveyed agreed that there might be a cut in interest rates towards the second half of 1997, if the mildly contractionary fiscal policy announced in the 1997 budget unveiled in October, eases the burden on monetary policy.
"There is a slowdown in Malaysia which should provide room for monetary easing, given that we have seen further tightening in fiscal policy," said Sim Moh Siong, economist with Citibank in Singapore.
"But the cut in interest rates will be small because the economic growth in Malaysia looks well supported. The easing is going to come later rather than sooner." he said

Malaysia's growing current account deficit and rising inflation had triggered worries about an overheating economy last year and forced the nation to maintain a tight monetary policy. The three-month interbank rate has risen by nearly 200 basis points in the last two years.
Malaysia expects to slow down the growth of its gross domestic product (GDP) to 8.2 percent for 1996 from 9.5 percent in 1995, making it the ninth successive year of over eight percent growth.
